interviewQuestions.question: How would you derive the time complexity of a recursive function you just wrote?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I write down its recurrence relation first, then solve that instead of trying to trace execution by hand.

To write T(n): I look at every recursive call in the function, note what size input each one gets (n/2? n-1? two calls or one?), and add the non-recursive work done at that same call level — a comparison, a loop, a merge step. For merge sort that's two calls on n/2 plus an O(n) merge: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n).

To solve it, I draw the recursion tree: figure out how many levels deep it goes, and how much total work happens at each level. For merge sort, the input halves each level (log n levels), and doubling nodes exactly cancels halving work-per-node, so every level costs O(n) — sum that across log n levels and you get O(n log n).

The one trap I watch for is confusing 'shrinks by a fraction' with 'shrinks by a fixed amount' — T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) is O(n log n), but T(n)=2T(n-1)+O(1), which also branches twice, is O(2ⁿ) because subtracting 1 gives n levels instead of log n.

**Testing:** whether you can set up and solve a recurrence rather than guessing complexity by analogy to a similar-looking algorithm.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci exponential when it only makes two recursive calls per invocation — the same branching factor as merge sort?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Branching factor alone doesn't determine complexity — what matters is branching factor **combined with how fast the tree gets shallow**, and those two recurrences differ exactly there.

Merge sort's calls are on n/2 and n/2: the input halves every level, so the tree is only log n levels deep before hitting the base case. Doubling the node count log n times caps out at O(n) leaves.

Fibonacci's calls are on n-1 and n-2: the input shrinks by a fixed amount, not a fraction, so the tree is n levels deep, not log n. Doubling the node count n times — not log n times — gives roughly 2ⁿ leaves, almost all of them recomputing the same smaller subproblems over and over (fib(5) gets recomputed independently dozens of times inside fib(10)'s tree).

Concretely, fib(30) makes millions of calls and fib(40) makes over a trillion — a 10-level increase in depth multiplies the work roughly a thousand-fold, which is the signature of 2ⁿ. That massive redundancy — the same subproblem solved repeatedly — is also exactly what memoization fixes: caching each distinct fib(k) collapses the tree to n unique subproblems, dropping it to O(n).

**Testing:** whether you understand that shrink rate, not branch count alone, determines whether a doubling recurrence is polynomial or exponential.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Recursion trees

interviewQuestions.question: When would you reach for the Master Theorem instead of drawing out the recursion tree by hand?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
In an interview, I'd almost always draw the tree first — it's the technique that visibly shows *why* an answer is what it is, which is what's actually being evaluated. I'd reach for the Master Theorem as a fast sanity check once the recurrence has the clean divide-and-conquer shape T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n): compare how fast the branching grows the leaf count, n^(log_b a), against how fast the per-call work f(n) grows, and whichever wins decides the answer.

Where it earns its keep is spotting non-obvious cases quickly — for instance recognizing that T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n) is dominated by the leaves (branching wins, giving O(n²)) versus T(n) = 4T(n/2) + O(n²) where the root's own work matches the leaf total exactly (giving O(n² log n)). Working those out by hand from the tree is fine but slower.

Where it doesn't apply at all: recurrences that don't fit the a·T(n/b) + f(n) shape, like Fibonacci's T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1) — different-sized subproblems, fixed shrink instead of fractional. There I go straight to the tree or a substitution argument; forcing the Master Theorem onto a shape it doesn't cover is a common error.

**Testing:** whether you know the Master Theorem's actual scope, versus treating it as a universal recurrence-solving hammer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Technique selection

interviewQuestions.question: A candidate claims their recursive solution is O(n) because it makes 'about n recursive calls total.' How do you push back on that reasoning?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd ask them what each individual call actually costs, because call count alone is only half the story — total work is calls multiplied by cost-per-call, and that second factor is rarely constant across a recursive tree.

Concretely: merge sort makes roughly O(n) total calls across its whole tree, but the calls near the root each do O(n)-ish work in their merge step, while calls near the leaves do almost none. Summing call count alone — 'O(n) calls, so O(n) time' — silently assumes every call costs the same, which understates the true O(n log n) by ignoring that the expensive calls are also the ones covering the most elements.

The correct move is the recursion-tree sum: total work per level, summed across levels, rather than total calls times an assumed constant. I'd walk through their specific function with them — find the non-recursive work at a call near the root versus one near a leaf, show that it scales with the slice size rather than being fixed, and recompute the real total from there.

This comes up most often exactly with divide-and-conquer code, where the 'combine' step (merge, partition, concatenation) is the part people forget to fold into the recurrence.

**Testing:** whether you can catch a plausible-sounding but wrong complexity argument and correct it with the right method, not just intuition.
